text: Welcome to Chapter Four of ServiceNow Performance and Troubleshooting. This lesson introduces the Instance Health dashboard — a tool that asks a very different question than the Slow Request Log you learned back in Chapter One, and knowing which one to reach for matters a lot in practice.

The Slow Request Log answers how slow was this one request, and where did the time go. Instance Health asks something else entirely: is the instance, as a whole, trending slower over the last week than it was last month. No single transaction record can answer that question, no matter how many of them you read one at a time — you need a view that aggregates across the whole instance and tracks it over time, and that's exactly what Instance Health is built to provide.

Instance Health continuously tracks three core metrics: response times across the instance, transaction volume, and error rates. Watched together over time, they tell a story no single number can. A climbing response time with rising volume might just mean the business is busier than usual. A climbing response time with flat or falling volume is a much more concerning signal that something about the platform itself has degraded.

The defining trait here is the time axis. An eight hundred millisecond response time means nothing on its own — is that good or bad? Instance Health's value comes from comparison — this week against last week, this hour against the same hour yesterday. That comparison is what turns a plain number into an actual, useful signal you can act on.

Mixing these two tools up wastes real diagnostic time. One slow incident form reported right now calls for the Slow Request Log, not Instance Health, because Instance Health has nothing to say about one specific transaction. A sense that the whole instance has felt sluggish for days calls for Instance Health instead, rather than hours spent reconstructing a trend by hand from dozens of isolated records.

Knowing which question you're actually being asked — why was this one thing slow, versus is everything trending slower across the instance — is what tells you which tool to open first, and that choice is the real skill this lesson is teaching. Next up, we'll look at semaphores and how a shared pool of node capacity gets rationed across competing work.
